title: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1)
hook: David weeps for Saul, who hunted him, and for Jonathan
carry: swifter than eagles, stronger than lions

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abigail on the hillside path, who kept David from avenging himself. Your line was blessed be your wisdom.

A man runs into David's camp with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. He comes from the battle on Mount Gilboa, carrying a crown and a bracelet. Saul's. The king is dead, he says, and Jonathan with him. Saul hunted David through caves and wilderness. Now the throne is open, and a man in David's position might feel relief. Instead David takes hold of his own clothes and tears them, and so do all the men with him. They mourn, and weep, and fast until evening, for Saul, for Jonathan, and for the people. Then David sings.

The song is a lament, and the text says it is written in the book of Jasher. Its refrain, in the King James Bible: "The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!" He doesn't want the news spread among the enemy: "Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon." He curses the mountains where they fell. And then he praises Saul. Not a word about the spears, the caves, the running. He tells the women of Israel to weep over Saul, who clothed them in scarlet. He sings of the two together: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions." Some readers call it generous. Some call it political: a new king honoring the old one. The text doesn't settle it. What it does is let David grieve the whole man, the king he was, not only the enemy he became. Then the song turns personal: "I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful." Two kinds of grief sit side by side: clean grief for a friend, and tangled grief for someone who did harm, and was also brave, and was also family. The refrain comes back at the end: how are the mighty fallen. One song, big enough to hold both.
screen: `A LAMENT, WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF JASHER.`
`DAVID PRAISES THE MAN WHO HUNTED HIM.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind whose loss is tangled: someone who hurt you and also gave you something, or someone gone you never quite made peace with; if no one comes, choose someone whose life you're grieving while they're alive. Don't tidy them up; let both be true, and find one honest good thing to say about them, as David did. If you pray, hold them before God without a verdict.
Jasher. The book that preserved David's lament for Saul, who hunted him, and for Jonathan, who loved him.
Your line: swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. One song for a friend and for a foe. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians read David's lament for Saul and Jonathan as a model of honest grief, and lines from it are sometimes read at funerals and memorials.

chat.says: Why would David write a sad song for Saul, who tried to kill him?
options: He grieved the whole man, the king Saul was, not only the enemy.
Saul had asked him, before the battle, to write a song for him.
He was glad Saul was gone, and sang it to celebrate his win.
chat.meaning: David's lament praises Saul and mourns Jonathan together, grieving the whole man, not only the enemy he became.

Gilboa.meaning: the mountain where Saul and Jonathan died in battle

Askelon.meaning: a Philistine city where David didn't want the news told

Gath.meaning: a Philistine city, among the enemy

notes: The messenger is an Amalekite who claims to have killed Saul at Saul's request (1:6–10); David has him executed (1:14–16). The script omits this for focus; Keeper to decide whether it should be named.
'The text says David ordered it taught to the people' is from 1:18 (the bow song, written in the book of Jasher); confirm wording.
The quotation from 1:26 stops before 'passing the love of women'. Some modern readers read the relationship as romantic; the script does not take a position.
Two readings of the praise of Saul (generous; political) are attributed to 'some readers'.
Original: refrain as in 1:19; confirm pointing and transliteration.

Editor: 'ordered it taught to the people' replaced with 'written in the book of Jasher' (1:18 in the KJV says 'teach the children of Judah the use of the bow', which is read differently); cut 'for years' and 'the years of running' (no span given in the text); pronunciation of נָפְלוּ corrected to naf-LOO; howItsDone softened to 'some Christians'.
